content: Miriam Lee was one of the pioneering acupuncturists in the United States and played a critical role in the legalization of acupuncture in California. She was born in China and worked as a nurse-midwife before transitioning to acupuncture. Miriam lived through the Second Sino-Japanese War and left mainland China in 1949. After leaving China, she resided in Singapore for 17 years before immigrating to the United States. When she arrived in California, acupuncture was illegal. To support herself, she worked on a factory assembly line while quietly providing acupuncture treatments from her home. Later, she collaborated with a supportive medical doctor and shared a clinical space. In 1974, Miriam Lee was arrested for practicing medicine without a license. During her trial, her patients filled the courtroom in protest, advocating for their right to access the only form of medicine that had effectively helped them. Shortly after, Governor Ronald Reagan legalized acupuncture as an experimental procedure. In 1976, Governor Jerry Brown signed legislation that permanently legalized acupuncture in California. That same year, Miriam Lee became one of the first licensed acupuncturists in the state. During the 1970s and early 1980s, Miriam Lee taught acupuncture to approximately 70% of the practitioners working in Northern California. She was renowned for her use of a specialized set of acupuncture points derived from the teachings of Dr. Tung, known as the Master Tung Magic Points. These points were later published in a book by Blue Poppy Press. Throughout her career, she remained innovative and dedicated to her practice. At the peak of her career, she treated up to 10 patients per hour and worked 80 hours a week. Miriam Lee popularized a 10-point protocol, which she detailed in her book, Insights of a Senior Acupuncturist. In this book, she described a combination of acupuncture points—ST36, SP6, LI4, LI11, and LU7—that have broad applications. This set of points, with slight modifications, has been shown to address many common complaints seen in Western acupuncture clinics by balancing the major organ systems. She also played a significant role in popularizing the Master Tung Magic Points, a nontraditional point system. In 1980, the Acupuncture Association of America was founded and led by Dr. Miriam Lee. The organization aimed to promote public education about acupuncture, provide continuing education for licensed practitioners, engage in legislative advocacy, and support acupuncture research.
